chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The word ENVIRONMENT is used very often on television, in newspapers and by people around us.
Our elders feel the environment is not what it used to be earlier.
Global summits involving developed and developing countries are regularly held to discuss ENVIRONMENTAL issues.
In this chapter we study how various components of the environment interact with each other and how we impact the environment.
The chapter looks in detail at two environmental problems: depletion of the OZONE LAYER and WASTE DISPOSAL.

chapter_sections.label: LIST OF TOPICS:
items: 13.2 How do our Activities Affect the Environment?
13.2.1 Ozone Layer and How it is Getting Depleted

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: DEFINITION: An ECOSYSTEM consists of all the interacting organisms in an area together with the non-living constituents of the environment. It is made up of BIOTIC components (living organisms) and ABIOTIC components (physical factors like temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: All organisms such as plants, animals, microorganisms and human beings, along with the physical surroundings, interact with each other and maintain a balance in nature.
BIOTIC COMPONENTS: living organisms — plants, animals, microorganisms.
ABIOTIC COMPONENTS: physical factors — temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals.

A garden is an ecosystem: it has grasses, trees, flower-bearing plants (rose, jasmine, sunflower) and animals (frogs, insects, birds) that interact and whose growth, reproduction and activities are affected by abiotic components.
NATURAL ECOSYSTEMS: forests, ponds and lakes (formed by nature).
HUMAN-MADE (ARTIFICIAL) ECOSYSTEMS: gardens and crop-fields (made by humans).
An aquarium is an example of a human-made ecosystem; adding aquatic plants and animals can make it a self-sustaining system.
Organisms are grouped by the manner in which they obtain their sustenance: PRODUCERS, CONSUMERS and DECOMPOSERS.

PRODUCERS (AUTOTROPHS): all green plants and certain bacteria that make organic compounds like sugar and starch from inorganic substances using radiant energy of the Sun in the presence of chlorophyll.
CONSUMERS: organisms which depend on producers, either directly or indirectly, for their food. They are classed as HERBIVORES, CARNIVORES, OMNIVORES and PARASITES.

DECOMPOSERS: microorganisms comprising bacteria and fungi that break down dead remains and waste products of organisms into simple inorganic substances that go into the soil and are used up again by plants.
Without decomposers, garbage, dead animals and plants would not break down and the natural replenishment of the soil would not take place.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.1:
sections.aim: To design an aquarium and understand it as a human-made ecosystem.
sections.materials: A large jar (or aquarium tank), water, oxygen pump (aerator), fish food, fish, aquatic plants and animals.
procedure: - Decide the things needed to create an aquarium: free space for swimming (a large jar), water, oxygen and food for the fish.
- Provide oxygen through an oxygen pump (aerator) and give fish food available in the market.
- Add a few aquatic plants and animals so it can become a self-sustaining system.
sections.observation: The aquarium has to be cleaned once in a while. A question is raised whether ponds or lakes have to be cleaned in the same manner, and why or why not.
sections.conclusion: An aquarium is a human-made ecosystem; with aquatic plants and animals it can become self-sustaining, but unlike natural ponds and lakes it needs cleaning because it lacks the natural balance of decomposers and other organisms found in nature.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.2:
sections.aim: To understand the interdependence of producers, consumers and decomposers and to form a food chain.
sections.materials: Information about the aquatic organisms in the aquarium created in Activity 13.1.
procedure: - Note whether, while creating the aquarium, care was taken not to put an aquatic animal that would eat others, and consider what would have happened otherwise.
- Make groups and discuss how each group of organisms (producers, consumers, decomposers) is dependent on the others.
- Write the aquatic organisms in the order of who eats whom and form a chain of at least three steps.
sections.observation: A chain of at least three steps can be formed showing one organism eating another.
sections.conclusion:
The organisms are interdependent. One group cannot be considered the only one of primary importance, because each group depends on the others to maintain the balance of the ecosystem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is an ecosystem? Name its two main components.
items.answer:
An ECOSYSTEM consists of all the interacting organisms in an area together with the non-living constituents of the environment.
Its two main components are:
- BIOTIC components — living organisms.
- ABIOTIC components — physical factors like temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals.

items.question: Differentiate between natural and artificial ecosystems with one example each.
items.answer:
- NATURAL ECOSYSTEM: formed by nature without human help. Example — forest, pond, lake.
- ARTIFICIAL (HUMAN-MADE) ECOSYSTEM: created and maintained by human beings. Example — garden, crop-field, aquarium.

items.question: Who are decomposers? State their role in the ecosystem.
items.answer:
DECOMPOSERS are microorganisms comprising bacteria and fungi.
Role:
- They break down the dead remains and waste products of organisms.
- They convert complex organic substances into simple inorganic substances.
- These inorganic substances go back into the soil and are used up again by the plants, helping in the natural replenishment of the soil.

items.question: Classify the organisms of an ecosystem on the basis of how they obtain food. Explain each.
items.answer:
On the basis of how they obtain their sustenance, organisms are grouped into three:
- PRODUCERS (Autotrophs): green plants and certain bacteria that make organic compounds (sugar, starch) from inorganic substances using sunlight in the presence of chlorophyll.
- CONSUMERS: organisms that depend on producers directly or indirectly for food; classed as herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and parasites.
- DECOMPOSERS: bacteria and fungi that break down dead remains and waste into simple inorganic substances returned to the soil.

items.question: An aquarium is called a human-made ecosystem. Justify, and explain why it needs cleaning while a pond does not.
items.answer:
- An aquarium has biotic components (fish, aquatic plants, animals) and abiotic components (water, oxygen, light), all created and maintained by humans, so it is a human-made ecosystem.
- With aquatic plants and animals it can become a self-sustaining system.
- However, it has to be cleaned once in a while because it lacks the full natural balance of decomposers and other organisms.
- A natural pond does not need such cleaning because it has decomposers and a self-regulating balance that recycles waste naturally.

items.question: Describe the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem and explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers with examples.
items.answer:
An ecosystem consists of biotic and abiotic components that interact to maintain a balance in nature.
- ABIOTIC COMPONENTS: non-living physical factors such as temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals. They affect the growth, reproduction and activities of living organisms.
- BIOTIC COMPONENTS: all living organisms — plants, animals, microorganisms. They are grouped as:
(i) PRODUCERS — green plants and certain bacteria that make food from inorganic substances using sunlight and chlorophyll (e.g. grass, trees).
(ii) CONSUMERS — organisms depending on producers directly or indirectly; herbivores (e.g. deer), carnivores (e.g. tiger), omnivores and parasites.
(iii) DECOMPOSERS — bacteria and fungi that break down dead remains and waste into simple inorganic substances returned to the soil.
Example: In a garden, grasses and trees (producers) are eaten by insects and frogs (consumers); when organisms die, bacteria and fungi (decomposers) break them down, recycling nutrients. Thus all components are interdependent and maintain balance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which of the following is a biotic component of an ecosystem?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Bacteria are living organisms, hence biotic. Temperature, soil and rainfall are non-living abiotic factors.

items.question: Producers in an ecosystem are also called:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Producers make their own food using sunlight, so they are autotrophs. The other terms refer to organisms that depend on producers.

items.question: Which of the following is a human-made ecosystem?
items.answer: D
items.explanation: Gardens and crop-fields are created and maintained by humans. Forests, ponds and lakes are natural ecosystems.

items.question: Bacteria and fungi that break down dead remains into simple inorganic substances are called:
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Decomposers break down dead matter and recycle nutrients into the soil. Producers make food and consumers eat other organisms.

items.question: Green plants make organic compounds from inorganic substances using sunlight in the presence of:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Chlorophyll captures the radiant energy of the Sun for photosynthesis. The other options are not the light-trapping pigment.

items.question: An aquarium with fish, plants, water and an aerator best represents:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: An aquarium is created by humans and, with aquatic plants and animals, can become self-sustaining. It contains both biotic and abiotic components, so options C and D are wrong.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A series of organisms feeding on one another forms a FOOD CHAIN.
Each step or level of the food chain forms a TROPHIC LEVEL.
TROPHIC LEVELS:
(i) First trophic level — AUTOTROPHS / PRODUCERS, which fix solar energy and make it available for heterotrophs.
(ii) Second trophic level — HERBIVORES / PRIMARY CONSUMERS.
(iii) Third trophic level — small carnivores / SECONDARY CONSUMERS.
(iv) Fourth trophic level — larger carnivores / TERTIARY CONSUMERS.
The interactions among components involve a FLOW OF ENERGY from one component to another.

Autotrophs capture energy present in sunlight and convert it into chemical energy; this energy supports all activities of the living world; from autotrophs energy goes to heterotrophs and decomposers.
When one form of energy is changed to another, some energy is lost to the environment in forms which cannot be used again.
Green plants in a terrestrial ecosystem capture about 1% of the energy of sunlight falling on their leaves and convert it into food energy.

When green plants are eaten by primary consumers, a great deal of energy is lost as heat, some goes into digestion and doing work, and the rest goes towards growth and reproduction. An average of 10% of the food eaten is turned into its own body and made available for the next level of consumers.
This is called the TEN PERCENT LAW — 10% is the average value of organic matter at each step that reaches the next level of consumers.
Because so little energy is available for the next level, food chains generally consist of only THREE or FOUR steps; very little usable energy remains after four trophic levels.
There are generally a greater number of individuals at the lower trophic levels; the greatest number is of the producers.

From the energy flow diagram (Fig. 13.4), the FLOW OF ENERGY IS UNIDIRECTIONAL — energy captured by autotrophs does not revert to solar input, and energy passed to herbivores does not come back to autotrophs.
The energy available at each trophic level gets diminished progressively due to loss of energy at each level.

BIOLOGICAL MAGNIFICATION: harmful chemicals (like pesticides) enter the food chain. They are washed into the soil or water, absorbed by plants and aquatic plants, and as they are not degradable they get accumulated progressively at each trophic level. Since human beings occupy the top level in any food chain, the maximum concentration of these chemicals gets accumulated in our bodies.
This is why food grains (wheat, rice), vegetables, fruits and even meat contain varying amounts of pesticide residues, which cannot always be removed by washing or other means.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.3:
sections.aim: To understand the source of pesticides in food and ways to reduce their intake.
sections.materials: Newspaper reports about pesticide levels in ready-made food items.
procedure: - Note that some states have banned certain products; debate in groups the need for such bans.
- Discuss what would be the source of pesticides in these food items and whether pesticides could get into our bodies from this source through other food products too.
- Discuss what methods could be applied to reduce our intake of pesticides.
sections.observation: Pesticides used on crops enter food items and reach our bodies through the food chain.
sections.conclusion: Pesticides enter food through their use on crops and accumulate in our bodies by biological magnification; their intake can be reduced by careful washing, choosing safer products and supporting reduced pesticide use.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is a food chain? Give one example.
items.answer:
A FOOD CHAIN is a series of organisms taking part at various biotic levels and feeding one on another.
Example: Grass to Deer to Tiger (grass eaten by deer, deer eaten by tiger).

items.question: What are trophic levels? Name them in order.
items.answer:
A TROPHIC LEVEL is each step or level of a food chain.
In order: Producers (first), Herbivores/Primary consumers (second), Secondary consumers (third) and Tertiary consumers (fourth).

items.question: State the ten percent law of energy flow. Why do food chains have only three or four steps?
items.answer:
- TEN PERCENT LAW: an average of only 10% of the food (energy) eaten at one trophic level is turned into the body of the consumer and made available to the next level; the rest is lost.
- Because so little energy is available for the next level, very little usable energy remains after four trophic levels, so food chains generally consist of only three or four steps.

items.question: Explain why the flow of energy in an ecosystem is said to be unidirectional.
items.answer:
- Energy captured by the autotrophs does not revert back to the solar input.
- Energy that passes to the herbivores does not come back to the autotrophs.
- As energy moves progressively through the various trophic levels, it is no longer available to the previous level.
- The energy available at each trophic level gets diminished progressively due to loss at each level. Hence the flow of energy is unidirectional.

items.question: What is biological magnification? Why is its level different at different trophic levels?
items.answer:
- BIOLOGICAL MAGNIFICATION is the progressive accumulation of harmful, non-degradable chemicals (such as pesticides) at each successive trophic level of a food chain.
- These chemicals enter through soil and water, are absorbed by plants, and pass up the food chain.
- As they are not degradable, their concentration increases at each higher level.
- Since human beings occupy the top level of the food chain, the maximum concentration accumulates in their bodies; thus the level is different (higher at higher trophic levels).

items.question: Distinguish between a food chain and a food web, and explain the flow of energy through trophic levels using the ten percent rule.
items.answer:
- A FOOD CHAIN is a single straight-line series of organisms feeding one on another (e.g., grass to deer to tiger).
- A FOOD WEB is a series of branching lines formed because each organism is eaten by two or more other kinds of organisms; thus many food chains interconnect.
- Flow of energy: autotrophs (producers) capture about 1% of sunlight and convert it to chemical energy at the first trophic level.
- When eaten by primary consumers, much energy is lost as heat, in digestion and work; only an average of 10% is stored and passed to the next level (TEN PERCENT LAW).
- This 10% transfer repeats at each level, so energy diminishes sharply.
- Because so little energy remains, food chains are limited to three or four steps, and the greatest number of individuals is at the producer level.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The first trophic level in a food chain is occupied by:
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Producers (autotrophs) fix solar energy and occupy the first trophic level. Herbivores and carnivores come at higher levels.

items.question: Which of the following is a correct food chain?
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Grass (producer) is eaten by goat (herbivore), which is eaten by human; this shows feeding levels. The others do not form a proper eat-and-be-eaten sequence.

items.question: According to the ten percent law, the energy transferred to the next trophic level is about:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: On average only 10% of the food energy is passed to the next level; the rest is lost as heat and in life processes.

items.question: The progressive accumulation of pesticides at higher trophic levels is called:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Non-degradable chemicals accumulate at each level, a process called biological magnification. The other terms describe unrelated phenomena.

items.question: Food chains generally consist of only three or four steps because:

options.B: Very little usable energy remains after four levels

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Since only about 10% of energy passes on at each step, very little usable energy is left after four trophic levels, limiting chain length.

items.question: In which trophic level does the maximum concentration of non-biodegradable pesticides accumulate?
items.answer: D
items.explanation: As chemicals are non-degradable and magnify up the chain, the top level (humans) accumulates the maximum concentration. Lower levels accumulate less.

topics.topic_name: HOW DO OUR ACTIVITIES AFFECT THE ENVIRONMENT?

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: 13.2.1 Ozone Layer and How it is Getting Depleted

DEFINITION: This topic studies how human beings, being an integral part of the environment, change the environment through their activities, focusing on two major environmental problems — depletion of the ozone layer and disposal of waste (garbage).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: We are an integral part of the environment; changes in the environment affect us and our activities change the environment around us.
Human activities pollute and alter the environment, as already seen in Class IX.
Two environmental problems are studied in detail: DEPLETION OF THE OZONE LAYER and WASTE DISPOSAL.
Waste materials we generate may be BIODEGRADABLE or NON-BIODEGRADABLE.
The disposal of the waste we generate is causing serious environmental problems.

items.question: Name the two environmental problems studied in detail in this topic.
items.answer:
The two environmental problems are:
- Depletion of the OZONE LAYER.
- WASTE DISPOSAL (managing the garbage we produce).

items.question: How do human activities affect the environment?
items.answer:
- We are an integral part of the environment, so our activities change the environment around us.
- Human activities pollute the environment and alter its balance, while changes in the environment in turn affect us.

items.question: Why is waste disposal becoming an increasingly serious problem?
items.answer:
- Improvements in our life-style have resulted in greater amounts of waste material generation.
- Changes in attitude and the increasing use of disposable things add to the waste.
- Changes in packaging have made much of our waste non-biodegradable, which persists and harms the environment, making disposal a serious problem.

items.question: Distinguish between biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances with examples.
items.answer:
- BIODEGRADABLE substances: broken down by biological processes (by bacteria and other saprophytes). Example — kitchen waste, vegetable peels, paper.
- NON-BIODEGRADABLE substances: not broken down by biological processes; may be inert and persist for a long time. Example — plastics.
- Biodegradable wastes are acted upon by decomposers; non-biodegradable wastes are acted upon only by physical processes like heat and pressure.
- Non-biodegradable substances harm the environment as they remain for very long periods.

items.question: Why will we not get any energy if we try to eat coal, and how is this related to biodegradability?
items.answer:
- Enzymes are specific in their action; a specific enzyme is needed to break down a particular substance.
- Our body does not have the enzyme to break down coal, so we get no energy from it.
- Similarly, many human-made materials like plastics cannot be broken down by bacteria or saprophytes because the required enzymes do not exist.
- Such materials are therefore non-biodegradable and persist in the environment for a long time.

items.question: Explain how our activities affect the environment with reference to ozone depletion and waste management.
items.answer:
Human beings are an integral part of the environment, and our activities change it in major ways.
- OZONE DEPLETION: the use of synthetic chemicals like CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons), used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers, has caused the amount of ozone in the atmosphere to drop sharply since the 1980s. Since the ozone layer shields the Earth from harmful UV radiation, its depletion is a serious concern (UV can cause skin cancer).
- WASTE MANAGEMENT: improvements in life-style and changes in packaging have increased waste, much of it non-biodegradable. Biodegradable waste is broken down by decomposers, but non-biodegradable waste (like plastics) persists and harms the ecosystem.
- Therefore both ozone depletion and improper waste disposal show how human activities seriously affect the environment, and steps like the 1987 UNEP agreement to freeze CFC production and proper waste segregation are needed to reduce the damage.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Substances that are broken down by biological processes are said to be:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Biodegradable substances are broken down by biological processes. Non-biodegradable, inert and synthetic materials resist such breakdown.

items.question: Which of the following is a non-biodegradable substance?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Plastics are not broken down by bacteria or saprophytes, so they are non-biodegradable. The others are biodegradable.

items.question: Why does the human body get no energy from eating coal?

options.B: No specific enzyme exists to break it down

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Enzymes are specific; our body lacks an enzyme to break down coal, so no energy is obtained. Coal is in fact non-biodegradable.

items.question: The increasing amount of non-biodegradable waste is mainly due to:

options.B: Changes in packaging and disposable items

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Modern packaging and disposable items have made much of our waste non-biodegradable. The other options reduce, not increase, such waste.

items.question: Which of the following groups contains only biodegradable items?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Fruit-peels, cake and lime-juice are all broken down biologically. The other groups contain plastic or leather, which are non-biodegradable or very slow to degrade. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

sections.label: EXERCISE 13.2 (In-text QUESTIONS box - textbook page 109, end of Topic 13.2 / before Exercises)

items.question: What is ozone and how does it affect any ecosystem?
items.answer: Ozone (O3) is a molecule formed by three atoms of oxygen. At the higher levels of the atmosphere it forms a layer that shields the Earth's surface from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun. It thus protects all organisms of the ecosystem from UV damage (UV can cause skin cancer); depletion of the ozone layer exposes the ecosystem to harmful UV radiation. (At ground level, however, ozone is a deadly poison.)

items.question: How can you help in reducing the problem of waste disposal? Give any two methods.
items.answer:
Two methods to reduce waste disposal problems:
- Reduce the use of disposable and non-biodegradable items (such as plastics), and reuse/recycle materials wherever possible.
- Segregate biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes so they can be treated and disposed of separately and properly.

subtopics.subtopic_name: OZONE LAYER AND HOW IT IS GETTING DEPLETED

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: While O2 (molecular oxygen) is essential for all aerobic forms of life, OZONE is a deadly poison at ground level.
However, at the higher levels of the atmosphere, ozone performs an essential function: it shields the Earth's surface from UV radiation from the Sun.
UV radiation is highly damaging to organisms; for example, it is known to cause SKIN CANCER in human beings.
FORMATION OF OZONE: higher-energy UV radiation acts on oxygen (O2) molecules and splits them into free oxygen (O) atoms. These atoms then combine with molecular oxygen to form ozone:
O2 --UV--> O + O
O + O2 --> O3 (Ozone)
The amount of ozone in the atmosphere began to drop sharply in the 1980s.
This decrease has been linked to synthetic chemicals like CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs), which are used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers.
In 1987, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) succeeded in forging an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels.
It is now mandatory for all manufacturing companies to make CFC-free refrigerators throughout the world.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.4:
sections.aim: To find out which chemicals deplete the ozone layer and whether regulations have controlled the damage.
sections.materials: Library books, internet access or newspaper reports.
procedure: - Find out from the library, internet or newspaper reports which chemicals are responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer.
- Find out if the regulations put in place to control the emission of these chemicals have succeeded in reducing the damage to the ozone layer.
- Find out whether the size of the hole in the ozone layer has changed in recent years.
sections.observation: Chemicals like CFCs are found to be responsible for ozone depletion, and regulations such as freezing CFC production aim to reduce the damage.
sections.conclusion: Synthetic chemicals like CFCs deplete the ozone layer; international regulations (like the freeze on CFC production) have been put in place to control emissions and reduce the size of the ozone hole.

items.question: What is ozone? How is it different from oxygen at ground level?
items.answer:
OZONE (O3) is a molecule formed by three atoms of oxygen.
At ground level, oxygen (O2) is essential for all aerobic life, but ozone is a deadly poison.

items.question: Why is the ozone layer important for life on Earth?
items.answer:
- The ozone layer at the higher levels of the atmosphere shields the Earth's surface from ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun.
- UV radiation is highly damaging to organisms; for example, it can cause skin cancer in human beings.

items.question: Explain how ozone is formed in the upper atmosphere.
items.answer:
- Higher-energy UV radiation acts on molecular oxygen (O2) and splits it into free oxygen (O) atoms:
O2 --UV--> O + O
- These free oxygen atoms then combine with molecular oxygen to form ozone:
O + O2 --> O3 (Ozone)
- Thus ozone is continuously produced at higher levels of the atmosphere by the action of UV radiation on oxygen.

items.question: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern? What steps are being taken to limit this damage?
items.answer:
- The ozone layer protects the Earth from harmful UV radiation; its damage exposes organisms to UV, which can cause skin cancer and harm to other living beings, so it is a serious concern.
- The amount of ozone began dropping sharply in the 1980s, linked to CFCs used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers.
- In 1987, UNEP forged an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels.
- It is now mandatory for all manufacturing companies worldwide to make CFC-free refrigerators.

items.question: What are CFCs? How are they related to ozone depletion?
items.answer:
- CFCs (CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS) are synthetic chemicals used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers.
- The amount of ozone in the atmosphere began to drop sharply in the 1980s.
- This decrease has been linked to CFCs, which release substances that destroy ozone.
- To control this, an international agreement (1987, UNEP) froze CFC production, and CFC-free refrigerators are now mandatory.

items.question: Describe the formation, importance and depletion of the ozone layer, and the measures taken to protect it.
items.answer:
- FORMATION: At higher levels of the atmosphere, UV radiation splits oxygen molecules (O2 --UV--> O + O), and the free O atoms combine with O2 to form ozone (O + O2 --> O3).
- IMPORTANCE: The ozone layer shields the Earth's surface from harmful UV radiation, which is highly damaging to organisms and can cause skin cancer; thus it protects the entire ecosystem.
- DEPLETION: The amount of ozone began to drop sharply in the 1980s, linked to synthetic chemicals like CFCs used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers.
- MEASURES: In 1987, UNEP forged an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels, and it is now mandatory for manufacturers worldwide to make CFC-free refrigerators, helping to reduce further depletion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Ozone is a molecule made up of how many oxygen atoms?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Ozone is O3, made of three oxygen atoms. Two atoms make ordinary oxygen (O2).

items.question: The ozone layer protects the Earth from:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: The ozone layer shields the Earth from harmful UV radiation. The other types are not blocked by ozone in this way.

items.question: Which chemicals are mainly responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer?
items.answer: B
items.explanation: CFCs, used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers, deplete the ozone layer. The other gases are not the main cause.

items.question: In which year did UNEP forge an agreement to freeze CFC production?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: In 1987 UNEP succeeded in forging an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels. 1986 is the reference year for the freeze, not the agreement year.

items.question: At ground level, ozone is best described as:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: At ground level ozone is a deadly poison; only at higher levels of the atmosphere does it perform the protective function. Oxygen (O2), not ozone, is essential for breathing.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: In our daily activities we generate a lot of material that is thrown away as waste.

Waste materials include kitchen waste (spoilt food, vegetable peels, used tea leaves, milk packets, empty cartons), waste paper, empty medicine bottles/strips/bubble packs, old and torn clothes and broken footwear.

The food we eat is digested by various enzymes in our body; ENZYMES ARE SPECIFIC in their action, so a specific enzyme is needed to break down a particular substance (that is why we get no energy if we try to eat coal).
Because of enzyme specificity, many human-made materials like plastics cannot be broken down by bacteria or other saprophytes.
Such materials are acted upon only by physical processes like heat and pressure, but under the ambient conditions of our environment they persist for a long time.
BIODEGRADABLE substances: substances that are broken down by biological processes.

NON-BIODEGRADABLE substances: substances that are not broken down by biological processes; they may be inert and simply persist in the environment for a long time or may harm the various members of the ecosystem.
Improvements in life-style have resulted in greater amounts of waste material generation.
Changes in attitude and the use of more disposable things, and changes in packaging, have resulted in much of our waste becoming non-biodegradable.
Proper management requires segregation of biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste and treatment of wastes by local bodies and industries.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.5:
sections.aim: To find out which waste materials are biodegradable and which are non-biodegradable, and which change fastest.
sections.materials: Waste material from homes (kitchen waste, waste paper, medicine bottles/strips, old clothes, broken footwear), a pit or an old bucket/flower pot, soil, water.
procedure: - Collect all the waste generated during a day from your homes.
- Bury this material in a pit in the school garden, or if there is no space, collect it in an old bucket/flower pot and cover with at least 15 cm of soil.
- Keep this material moist and observe at 15-day intervals.
sections.observation:
- Note which materials remain unchanged over long periods of time.
- Note which materials change their form and structure over time.
- Note which of the changed materials change the fastest.
sections.conclusion: Some materials (biodegradable, like kitchen waste and paper) change and break down over time, while others (non-biodegradable, like plastics) remain unchanged for long periods; biodegradable wastes change faster.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.6:
sections.aim: To find out more about biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances.
procedure: - Use the library or internet to find out more about biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances.
- Find out how long various non-biodegradable substances are expected to last in our environment.
- Find out about new types of plastics said to be biodegradable, and whether they harm the environment.
sections.observation: Non-biodegradable substances last for very long periods; some newer plastics are claimed to be biodegradable.
sections.conclusion: Non-biodegradable substances persist for very long times and harm the environment, while newly developed biodegradable plastics may reduce this harm, though their actual effect must be checked.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.7:
sections.aim: To study how waste generated at home is collected and treated.
sections.materials: Information from home and from the local body (panchayat, municipal corporation, resident welfare association).
procedure: - Find out what happens to the waste generated at home and whether there is a system in place to collect it.
- Find out how the local body deals with the waste and whether there are mechanisms to treat biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes separately.
- Calculate how much waste is generated at home in a day and how much of it is biodegradable.
- Calculate how much waste is generated in the classroom in a day and how much of it is biodegradable.
- Suggest ways of dealing with this waste.
sections.observation: A measurable amount of waste is generated daily, part biodegradable and part non-biodegradable, and the local body may or may not treat them separately.
sections.conclusion: Waste should be collected systematically and biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes should be treated separately for proper management.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.8:
sections.aim: To study how sewage and industrial wastes in the locality are treated.
sections.materials: Information about the local sewage system and local industries.
procedure: - Find out how the sewage in your locality is treated and whether there are mechanisms to ensure that local water bodies are not polluted by untreated sewage.
- Find out how the local industries in your locality treat their wastes and whether there are mechanisms to ensure that the soil and water are not polluted by this waste.
sections.observation: Sewage and industrial wastes may or may not be treated before being released, affecting soil and water bodies.
sections.conclusion: Proper treatment of sewage and industrial waste is necessary to prevent pollution of soil and water bodies.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.9:
sections.aim: To find out how hazardous materials and plastics are dealt with during disposal and recycling.
procedure: - Search the internet or library to find out what hazardous materials have to be dealt with while disposing of electronic items and how they affect the environment.
- Find out how plastics are recycled and whether the recycling process has any impact on the environment.
sections.observation: Electronic items contain hazardous materials, and plastic recycling has its own environmental impacts.
sections.conclusion: Hazardous materials in e-waste must be handled carefully, and even plastic recycling can affect the environment, so safe disposal and recycling methods are important.

sections.label: EXERCISE 13.2.2:

items.question: Why are some substances biodegradable and some non-biodegradable?
items.answer: Biological breakdown depends on specific enzymes. Substances for which the right enzymes (in bacteria/saprophytes) exist are broken down and are biodegradable; human-made substances like plastics, for which no such enzymes exist, are not broken down and are non-biodegradable.

items.question: Give any two ways in which biodegradable substances would affect the environment.
items.answer:
- On decomposing they may produce foul smells and unhygienic conditions if not managed.
- Their decomposition by microorganisms releases nutrients back into the soil, enriching it (a beneficial effect) but can also cause pollution of water if dumped in excess.

items.question: Give any two ways in which non-biodegradable substances would affect the environment.
items.answer:
- They persist in the environment for a very long time, accumulating as waste and polluting soil and water.
- They may harm members of the ecosystem and, being non-degradable, cause biological magnification of harmful substances up the food chain.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS:
sections.text:
[Think it over box - page 108]
- DISPOSABLE CUPS IN TRAINS: Earlier, tea in trains was served in plastic glasses that had to be returned to the vendor. Disposable cups were introduced as a step forward for hygiene, but their disposal in millions on a daily basis caused problems. Some time back, KULHADS (disposable cups made of clay) were suggested as an alternative, but making them on a large scale would result in loss of fertile top-soil. Now disposable paper-cups are used. The advantages of disposable paper-cups over disposable plastic cups should be thought about (paper cups are biodegradable, while plastic cups are non-biodegradable).

items.question: Define biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances.
items.answer:
- BIODEGRADABLE substances: those that are broken down by biological processes (e.g. kitchen waste).
- NON-BIODEGRADABLE substances: those that are not broken down by biological processes and persist in the environment (e.g. plastics).

items.question: Why can plastics not be broken down by bacteria?
items.answer:
- Enzymes are specific in their action, and bacteria do not have the specific enzymes needed to break down plastics.
- Hence plastics are non-biodegradable and persist for a long time in the environment.

items.question: How can you help in reducing the problem of waste disposal? Give any three methods.
items.answer:
- Reduce the use of disposable and non-biodegradable items like plastics.
- Reuse and recycle materials wherever possible.
- Segregate biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes so each can be treated and disposed of properly.

items.question: What are the problems caused by the non-biodegradable wastes that we generate?
items.answer:
- Non-biodegradable wastes persist in the environment for very long periods and accumulate as garbage.
- They pollute the soil and water bodies.
- They may harm members of the ecosystem.
- Harmful non-degradable chemicals can undergo biological magnification, accumulating up the food chain and reaching humans.

items.question: If all the waste we generate is biodegradable, will this have no impact on the environment? Explain.
items.answer:
- Even biodegradable waste, if generated in very large amounts, can cause problems.
- Its decomposition can produce foul smells and unhygienic conditions and attract disease-carrying organisms.
- Excess biodegradable waste dumped in water bodies can pollute them and reduce oxygen for aquatic life.
- So even biodegradable waste does have an impact and must be managed properly.

items.question: Explain why waste management has become important, and suggest measures to manage the garbage we produce.
items.answer:
- Improvements in life-style and changes in packaging have greatly increased the amount of waste, much of it non-biodegradable.
- Non-biodegradable waste like plastics persists for a long time, pollutes soil and water, and harms the ecosystem, while excess biodegradable waste also causes unhygienic conditions.
- MEASURES:
(i) Reduce the use of disposable and non-biodegradable items.
(ii) Reuse and recycle materials.
(iii) Segregate biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes.
(iv) Ensure proper treatment of sewage and industrial wastes so soil and water are not polluted.
(v) Handle hazardous e-waste carefully.
- A change in attitude towards consumption and disposal is also necessary to manage garbage effectively.

items.question: Which of the following is a biodegradable waste?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Vegetable peels are broken down by microorganisms, hence biodegradable. Plastic, glass and aluminium are non-biodegradable.

items.question: Substances that are NOT broken down by biological processes are called:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: Such substances are non-biodegradable and persist in the environment. Biodegradable substances are broken down biologically.

items.question: Plastics are non-biodegradable because:

options.B: Specific enzymes to break them down do not exist

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Bacteria lack the specific enzymes needed to break down plastics, so they are not degraded biologically. The other statements are false.

items.question: Which of the following are environment-friendly practices?

options.A: Carrying cloth-bags to put purchases in while shopping
options.B: Switching off unnecessary lights and fans
options.C: Walking to school instead of using a vehicle

items.answer: D
items.explanation: All three reduce waste and conserve resources, so all are environment-friendly. Hence "All of the above" is correct.

items.question: Why were kulhads (clay cups) NOT a fully suitable alternative to disposable plastic cups?

options.B: Making them on a large scale causes loss of fertile top-soil

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Large-scale manufacture of clay kulhads would result in loss of fertile top-soil. Kulhads are actually biodegradable and do not release CFCs.

items.question: Which of the following groups contain only biodegradable items?
items.answer:
(a) Grass, flowers and leather
(b) Grass, wood and plastic
(c) Fruit-peels, cake and lime-juice
(d) Cake, wood and grass
ANSWER: (c) Fruit-peels, cake and lime-juice.
EXPLANATION: These are all broken down biologically. (Note: option (d) cake, wood and grass are also biodegradable; per NCERT/KSEEB key the intended answer is (c).)

items.question: Which of the following constitute a food-chain?
items.answer:
(a) Grass, wheat and mango
(b) Grass, goat and human
(c) Goat, cow and elephant
(d) Grass, fish and goat
ANSWER: (b) Grass, goat and human.
EXPLANATION: Grass (producer) to goat (herbivore) to human shows a proper feeding sequence. The others do not.

items.question: Which of the following are environment-friendly practices?
items.answer:
(a) Carrying cloth-bags to put purchases in while shopping
(b) Switching off unnecessary lights and fans
(c) Walking to school instead of getting your mother to drop you on her scooter
(d) All of the above
ANSWER: (d) All of the above.
EXPLANATION: Each option reduces waste or saves energy and resources.

items.question: What will happen if we kill all the organisms in one trophic level?
items.answer: If all organisms in one trophic level are killed, the balance of the ecosystem is disturbed. The organisms in the level below (their food source) would increase unchecked, while the organisms in the level above (which feed on them) would not get food and would decline or die. The whole food chain and energy flow would be disrupted.

items.question: Will the impact of removing all the organisms in a trophic level be different for different trophic levels? Can the organisms of any trophic level be removed without causing any damage to the ecosystem?
items.answer: Yes, the impact differs for different trophic levels because each level depends on those below and supports those above. No, organisms of any trophic level cannot be removed without causing damage, since all levels are interdependent and removing any one disturbs the energy flow and balance of the whole ecosystem.

items.question: What is biological magnification? Will the levels of this magnification be different at different levels of the ecosystem?
items.answer: BIOLOGICAL MAGNIFICATION is the progressive accumulation of harmful, non-degradable chemicals (like pesticides) at each successive trophic level of a food chain. Yes, the levels differ: the concentration increases at each higher trophic level, and is maximum at the top level (human beings), since these chemicals are not degraded and accumulate as they move up the chain.

items.question: What are the problems caused by the non-biodegradable wastes that we generate?
items.answer: Non-biodegradable wastes persist in the environment for a very long time, pollute the soil and water bodies, and harm members of the ecosystem. Harmful non-degradable chemicals in them can undergo biological magnification, accumulating up the food chain and ultimately reaching human beings.

items.question: If all the waste we generate is biodegradable, will this have no impact on the environment?
items.answer: No, even fully biodegradable waste will have an impact if generated in large amounts. Its decomposition produces foul smells and unhygienic conditions and can attract disease-causing organisms. Excess biodegradable waste dumped into water bodies can pollute them and reduce dissolved oxygen, harming aquatic life. Hence biodegradable waste must also be managed properly.

items.question: Why is damage to the ozone layer a cause for concern? What steps are being taken to limit this damage?
items.answer: Damage to the ozone layer is a cause for concern because the ozone layer protects the Earth from harmful UV radiation, which can cause skin cancer and other damage to organisms. Steps to limit the damage: in 1987 UNEP forged an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels, and it is now mandatory for all manufacturing companies worldwide to make CFC-free refrigerators.

sections.label: WHAT YOU HAVE LEARNT
sections.text:
- The various components of an ecosystem are interdependent.
- The producers make the energy from sunlight available to the rest of the ecosystem.
- There is a loss of energy as we go from one trophic level to the next; this limits the number of trophic levels in a food-chain.
- Human activities have an impact on the environment.
- The use of chemicals like CFCs has endangered the ozone layer. Since the ozone layer protects against the ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, this could damage the environment.
- The waste we generate may be biodegradable or non-biodegradable.
- The disposal of the waste we generate is causing serious environmental problems.
